title: I've Loved You So Long
full_review:
Currently earning rapturous reviews on Broadway for her mercurial performance in Anton Chekhov's "The Seagull," Kristin Scott Thomas shows a vastly different aspect of her talent in a moving film from France, the English actress's adopted country.

In "I've Loved You So Long" (Sony Classics), she plays Juliette, a chain-smoking broken woman released from prison after 15 years for having inexplicably murdered her 6-year-old child.

Her younger sister, Lea (Elsa Zylberstein), now a professor of literature, has insisted Juliette move in with her and husband Luc (Serge Hazanavicius), though he's wary of allowing Juliette under the same roof as their two young daughters, both adopted Vietnamese girls. Also in the household is Luc's stroke-victim father (Jean-Claude Arnaud), who can no longer speak yet seems to understand her ingrained detachment.

The taciturn Juliette must still report regularly to a parole officer (Frederic Pierrot) and, in a droll role reversal, he uses her as a soundboard for his troubles. Before long, she is allowed a job as a medical secretary, with the proviso that she not mention that she had been a doctor before her prison term.

Gradually, embraced by Lea and Luc's friends and the loving atmosphere of the household -- most especially by the children who come to love her -- Juliette has a sort of rebirth, coming to terms with her past and slowly learning to reconnect with the outside world.

The film is anchored by Thomas' extraordinary performance, her careworn face speaking volumes in the film's many close-ups, and her inner transformation wonderfully natural and credible.

Though her central character dominates the film, she's beautifully matched by Zylberstein, as the pair re-establishes a sisterly bond thought lost. Lea's seeming equanimity masks inner turmoil as we finally see when Lea lashes out at her students who discourse so knowingly on Dostoevsky and his characters' redemption, when, in fact, they know nothing of life.

Novelist-turned-director Philippe Claudel's compassionate story demonstrates profound respect for human dignity. As the characters come to know Juliette as a person, their preconceptions recede, and genuine understanding takes their place.

In French. Subtitles.

The film contains an implied nonmarital encounter, suicide, a couple of crude expressions. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. Not rated by the Motion Picture Association of America.
